the group delay and origin of the RW CM are not consistent with a cochlear-base origin of the lowfrequency RW CM.

the cochlear group delay of RW CM provides no information on cochlear wave propagation and that the generation site for low-frequency RW CM changes from the apex to the cochlear base with increasing sound levels.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the low-frequency CM is generated by the auditory nerve, not by the cochlear partition, and the RW CM is a mixture of CM and neurophonic potentials.
the low-frequency RW potential is not a cochlear microphone but rather a neurophonic potential, and its generation is shifted from the apex to the base as the sound level increases.
low-frequency RW CM is not a pure cochlear microphone potential.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in gerbils, the RW CM below ∼1 kHz is dominated by the auditory nerve neurogenic potential and the RW CM above ∼2 kHz is dominated by cochlear microphonics generated at the cochlea base.
, at high sound level, low-frequency CM is dominated by a cochlear-base origin, while at low or intermediate levels, it is dominated by an apex-origin.
the low-frequency RW microphonic potential is not a pure cochlear potential, but a mixture of the neurophonic potential and the cochlear microphonics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
low-frequency RW CM cannot be used as an index for the cochlear base integrity.
the RW CM is not a reliable measure of cochlear mechanics at the cochlear apex.
the RW CM recorded at low sound levels should not be used for evaluating cochlear mechanics or for studying wave propagation inside the scala tympani.
